current_example.title: Example: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

q-31596.name: Question 1
q-31596.worked_solution:
Note that plugging in $x=0$ gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[x\operatorname{cos}⁡x]^{′}}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{(\frac{1}{x+1})} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0}{(\frac{1}{0+1})} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-31600.name: Question 2
q-31600.worked_solution:
Note that plugging in $x=-1$ gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}{{x}^{2}+3x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}+3x+2]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)+\frac{x}{x+2})}{2x+3} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1+2)+\frac{-1}{-1+2})}{2(-1)+3} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-1}{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

q-336911.name: Question 3
q-336911.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)]}^{′}}{[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}^{′}}{{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{16\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} \\  & =4{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{1-0} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-114252.name: Question 4
q-114252.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x{e}^{-x}-x+2{x}^{2}}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[x{e}^{-x}-x+2{x}^{2}]^{′}}{[{sin}^{2}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x{e}^{-x}-x+2{x}^{2}}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x]^{′}}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡2x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(x-2){e}^{-x}+4}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x} \\  & =\frac{(0-2){e}^{0}+4}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =\frac{-2+4}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-336901.name: Question 5
q-336901.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=3$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+9}{16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{[{x}^{2}-6x+9]}^{′}}{[16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{2x-6}{(\frac{8}{\sqrt{x+1}}-4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{4(x+1)^{-1/2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+9}{16\sqrt{x+1}-4x-20} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{4(x+1)^{-1/2}-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{[x-3]}^{′}}{{[4(x+1)^{-1/2}-2]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{1}{-2(x+1)^{-3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 3}(x+1)^{3/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(3+1)^{3/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72339.name: Question 6
q-72339.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)]}^{′}}{[\operatorname{csc}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cancel{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

limx→0+ln⁡(sin⁡x)csc⁡x=limx→0+[ln⁡(sin⁡x)]′[csc⁡x]′=limx→0+cot⁡x−csc⁡xcot⁡x=−limx→0+cot⁡xcsc⁡xcot⁡x=−limx→0+1csc⁡x=−limx→0+sin⁡x=0.

q-336802.name: Question 7
q-336802.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)=-\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{-\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)}{ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)} & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{[ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)]}^{′}}{{[ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x})}{(-\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x}{{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}}{\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-336971.name: Question 8
q-336971.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[{x}^{3}]^{′}}{[{ln}^{2}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3{x}^{2}}{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3{x}^{3}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[3{x}^{3}]^{′}}{{[2\operatorname{ln}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{9{x}^{2}}{(\frac{2}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{9{x}^{3}}{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

q-3781.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields
